transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-09
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (CTO, Vela), Sana Patel (ML Eng), Jordan Lee (Platform Lead)

Summary:
Quick catalog demo focused on 'scouting' workflow — how Redwood's model catalog surface helps Vela shortlist open models, read benchmark signals, and decide on quantization / compatibility for Vela's latency-sensitive chat feature. Discussed hosted vs dedicated fit, VPC/private considerations, and next steps for a POC benchmark run on Vela infra.

Topics covered:
- Model discovery heuristics (quality vs cost)
- Benchmark interpretation (throughput/latency percentiles, prompt sets)
- Compatibility matrix (ops: kernels, quant profiles, sequence lengths)
- Routing and fallback policies for mixed variants
- Security and deployment constraints (VPC, KMS, SOC2)

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call — I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, Diego is our solutions engineer. Could you do a quick intro?
[00:08] Liam (Vela): Yeah hi, Liam O'Connor, CTO at Vela. We run a real-time customer chat assistant that needs sub-150ms tail token latency for short replies, and we're trying to figure out the best open models to use.
[00:16] Sana (Vela): Sana here, ML Eng — I'm mostly evaluating generation quality and hallucination behavior on our prompts.
[00:20] Jordan (Vela): Jordan, Platform — I'll own infra questions, network, and security.
[00:24] Diego (Redwood SE): Great, thanks. Quick agenda: we will show the catalog scouting UI, walk a compatibility matrix example, and then run through benchmark artifacts and what they mean — then Q&A and next steps.
[00:30] Maya: Cool. Note, parts of the transcript might have auto-captions fuzz — apologies if acronyms get munged.

[02:12] Maya: Okay opening the catalog — first thing is model filters. You can filter by architecture, token throughput, compatibility (FP16/INT8), and precomputed benchmarks for your prompt set. For Vela you'd likely look at short-seq profiles.
[02:45] Sana: How do you compute the benchmarks? Are these synthetic or real prompts?
[02:51] Diego: Good question. We store both representative open prompt suites — customers can upload their own prompt set. Benchmarks we show are twofold: Redwood-internal runner with standard prompts, and user-submitted runs. We also surface 95th/99th latency percentiles, as well as throughput under batching.
[03:10] Liam: So when you say "compatibility matrix" what columns should we expect?
[03:15] Diego: Typically: model variant, supported quant profiles, recommended kernel/hardware, memory footprint, expected latency at N tokens, and flags for KV cache behavior. We also show fallback compatibility — e.g., if INT8 artifact isn't available, what's the nearest FP16 variant.
[04:02] Jordan: Who generates the quant profiles? Can Redwood recommend quant for our A100s or for CPU offloads?
[04:08] Diego: We generate a recommended set based on model architecture and your target hardware. For A100 we usually recommend FP16 or AMP, for T4/RTX we provide INT8 post-training quant profiles with notes. We'll attach a quantization playbook.

[06:00] Maya: Demo time — filter for "short-context" and prefilter to open models only.
[06:12] Speaker 1: (background) loading...
[06:20] Diego: Here we have three candidates: OpenLlamax-20B (shaved name from caption), Mistral-7B, and Falcon-40B-cx. For Vela's latency targets, you could start with Mistral-7B quantized to INT8, or a distilled 13B with KV cache warmed.
[06:52] Sana: Distilled 13B — is that in your catalog as a variant or would we bring our own?
[06:58] Diego: Some distill variants are in catalog; others we can onboard. Onboarding takes a few steps — we validate the model, run a compatibility job to determine kernel runtime and memory, and then publish a catalog entry.

[09:10] Liam: The 99th percentile is the one that bites us. How do I interpret Redwood's 99th numbers? Is that measured with cold starts?
[09:20] Diego: We try to separate cold vs warm. Our 99th includes realistic traffic with batching and cache behavior. We also provide a cold-start column. For Vela's chat use-case you might set a policy to pin some warm instances (Dedicated) or use prefix caching to keep KV warm.
[09:45] Jordan: If we do Private (VPC), do we lose any of the catalog features?
[09:53] Maya: No — the catalog and optimize suggestions are part of the control plane; for Private deployments the control plane can run in the customer VPC. Some telemetry levels change based on security commitments — we can restrict analytics and keep run logs local.

[12:05] Sana: Another thing — hallucination checks. Does the catalog show qualitative evals or only latency/cost?
[12:12] Diego: We show both. There's a "quality" tab where we surface redwood-evals: prompt-level accuracy, hallucination rate on curated datasets, and an example prompt bank. You can also plug in your eval harness to evaluate candidate models and compare side-by-side.
[12:35] Liam: That's helpful. Can we upload our prompt set and have Redwood rerun the benches?
[12:40] Diego: Yes — you can upload a CSV up to X rows (we'll share limits) and we'll run a POC bench on hosted infra or we can run the runner against your dedicated nodes if you prefer private. That runner outputs per-prompt latency and per-token cost.

[15:01] Maya: Switching to the compatibility matrix page — note the matrix flags kernel mismatches. For example, Falcon-40B-cx has optimized fused kernels that improve tail latency, but those kernels are only available for certain CUDA/driver combos.
[15:25] Jordan: If our driver is behind, can Redwood provide fallback kernels?
[15:29] Diego: We ship fallback kernel paths and can build custom runtime images for you. The matrix will show which kernels will be used and whether it's expected to degrade latency by N%.

[18:02] Sana: About quantization: some of our prompts are sensitive to small weight changes. How do we evaluate quality/regression?
[18:10] Diego: Our Optimize tool ties quant recommendations to eval sets. You can run an A/B: run the prompt bank on FP16 vs INT8 and we'll compute quality deltas per prompt and aggregate. We also show where hallucination or token-level perplexity diverges.
[18:32] Liam: Could you show an example report?
[18:35] Diego: Showing one — here's a delta chart: most prompts are within 0.8% BLEU/ROUGE, but some edge cases show 4-6% drop and those are flagged for manual review.

[21:00] Speaker 2: (crosstalk)
[21:10] Maya: Quick pause: any legal or procurement blockers we should be aware of up front?
[21:15] Jordan: We'll need SOC2 Type II and a network diagram; also SSO/SAML integration for admin access. Data residency isn't critical yet but we do need KMS integration for keys.
[21:30] Maya: Good — we have SOC2 artifacts and a standard network diagram; we'll share the security pack. For KMS we support customer-managed keys and HSM workflows.

[24:00] Diego: Back to routing — the catalog can suggest model routing policies by cost vs latency. For example, route 95% of traffic to the INT8 Mistral-7B and fallback to FP16 13B when tokens exceed 256, or route long-context to a 40B variant.
[24:28] Sana: Do you have automatic rollout metrics? We don't want sudden quality regressions in prod.
[24:33] Diego: Console supports canary rollouts and automatic rollback if eval metrics cross thresholds. You can bind a prompt set as a regression sentinel.

[27:05] Liam: For our POC, we'd like to do two things: a shortlist and a short-run benchmark on our infra simulating 10 RPS with 90/10 short/long token distributions. How long would that take?
[27:20] Maya: If you provide sample traffic and access to a test cluster, we can run the baseline in 1-2 business days for the common candidates. Diego will prepare the script.
[27:35] Diego: I'll prepare a benchmark runner and a README. We can also simulate prefix caching and cold starts.

[30:12] Sana: About cost — does the catalog show per-token cost estimates including batching impact?
[30:20] Diego: Yep — we show per-token cost baked with typical batch sizes and host pricing options. For Dedicated we show effective per-token based on reserved capacity discounts. Optimize will also propose batching and cache settings that minimize unit cost while meeting tail latency.

[33:02] Jordan: Network egress concerns: if weights need to be pulled at startup, what's the best pattern?
[33:08] Diego: We recommend pre-staging weights on a local image or an internal S3 mirror; the onboarding runbook includes a weights-staging step. We'll document the recommended S3 presigned method vs image bake.

[35:45] Maya: Ok let's summarize next steps. We'll (1) share the compatibility CSV and quant notes, (2) send the security pack, (3) Diego will share the benchmark runner and schedule the POC run, (4) Vela will share sample traffic and test cluster details.
[36:10] Liam: Sounds good. Can we get an estimated cost for a 2-week POC?
[36:15] Maya: We'll put a rough estimate in the POC plan — depends on model choices and whether you use Hosted or Dedicated — we'll include options.

[38:00] Sana: A couple of quick clarifications — the eval harness, is that open-source?
[38:05] Diego: Yes, it's an open harness we provide links to; customers can run locally. The Console integrates the results if you upload the output.

[40:20] Speaker 3: (short audio glitch)
[40:30] Jordan: For SSO provisioning, we use Okta. Any known issues?
[40:34] Maya: Okta is supported, we have an SAML metadata exchange flow and can provision RBAC roles. We'll include a short SSO setup guide.

[43:02] Diego: One more note on matrix mismatches: sometimes the model has a CUDA extension we don't yet ship — we flag it and either suggest a kernel patch, or a different model variant. We try to avoid surprises in prod.

[45:12] Maya: Thanks all. We'll follow up with dates for the POC and the links. Anything else?
[45:22] Liam: Nope, thanks — we'll get those traffic files to Jordan and he will share them.
[45:30] Sana: Thanks everyone.
[45:34] Jordan: Thanks.
[45:40] Maya: Great — bye all.

End of transcript.
